about: Words for the chain york_954 (cards: Data/encounters/chain_york_954_793.json; page: Design/content/chains/york_954.md). York between the kings of Dublin, Eric son of Harald and the king of the English, 947 to 954. Keys: chain_york_954.<card>.<what>; an option's label is opt_<key> and its outcome out_<key> (out_<key>_fail for a failed chance); art.<card id> says what the card's picture shows. The two Chronicle lines are quoted from Ingram 1823; everything else is new. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: At York the king changes with the season: Olaf of Dublin, Eric son of Harald, or the English king. A safe-conduct there is good only while the king who gave it sits in the hall.
Dublin pays well for wine and for York jet, and sells hides, wool cloaks and captives. The road over the hills from York is its king's road.
Eric son of Harald was driven from York and killed on Stainmore with his son and his brother. King Eadred has the kingdom and Oswulf of Bamburgh is earl. There are no more kings at York.
Eric son of Harald was not killed when York drove him out. He went down the Ouse by night in a merchant's hull, and holds the islands north of the Scots with a fleet.
Olaf of Dublin, called Cuaran, holds York a third time: his ships came up the Humber before the English king's reeves. Eric son of Harald died on Stainmore.
Whose penny
At the landing below the bridge a moneyer's man turns your pennies over on a board. They carry the wrong king. A townsman watches and waits to be asked.
Good silver and the wrong face. I can weigh these or I can strike them. I cannot take them as they are.
At Tanshelf we swore to King Eadred, so it was his penny. Now Eric, Harald's son, is in the hall and I am cutting his name. Ask me again at Martinmas.
Ripon burned this year for the sake of one king, and we paid another to go home. The die on my bench is English again. I keep the old ones oiled.
Olaf is back from Dublin, so it is the knot and the banner. I have struck for him before. My hand knows the way.
A stranger here sells through a townsman or sells to the wind. I have a roof, a yard, and a name the bench knows. My cut is one penny in twelve.
Whose word did you come up the river on? Never mind. A king's word here lasts as long as the king. I have known cheeses that lasted longer.
Have forty pennies struck anew; the moneyer keeps six
Take the townsman's roof and trade through him
Ask who is king, and who was, and say nothing else
Forty pennies go into the pot and thirty-four come back, bright, with this season's king on them. The toll man takes them without biting one.
His name is Ulfketil: a Danish father, an English mother, and a yard behind the landing. Your goods go under his roof and his name goes on your sales.
He tells it on his fingers: Olaf, Olaf, Ragnall, Edmund, Eadred, Eric. He has fingers left, and nobody on the landing thinks he will not need them.
Three doors
Your host walks you through the town before the market opens. He stops three times: at the king's hall, at the minster gate, and at the Dublin ships.
Three doors in this town. Knock at one and the other two hear it. Knock at none and you pay full toll and sleep on your cargo.
The hall. Whoever sits in it wants wine and is short of it. The steward is the one man in there who is never changed.
I have poured for five kings in this hall. A gift laid on the table is remembered by the table, whoever sits at it.
Saint Peter's. The archbishop swore to the English king at Tanshelf and unswore before the hay was in. He is still archbishop. Think about that.
You are the one with the round hull. Sit. In Dublin they give a cow's price for what you sell here at a calf's. I say it for nothing.
Lay a gift of thirty pennies on the hall's table
Drink with the Dublin shipmaster on the landing
Stand witness for your host at the moneyers' bench, and be seen doing it
The steward counts the gift twice and names what the hall will pay for six casks of Rhine wine: half as much again as the market. He sends you off with a riddle the king's men ask over their cups.
Gilli's mother was Irish and the ship was his father's. By the bottom of the jug you know what wine fetches on the Liffey, and he knows your name.
You stand at the bench while his silver is weighed and say aloud what you saw. Four townsmen nod. It is a small thing and they will remember it.
The price of a king
The town owes King Eadred silver for having taken another king. A clerk with a tally goes from hull to hull along the landing, and he has reached yours.
You saw the smoke over Ripon. That was Wilfrid's church. Eadred said he would come back and burn the rest, so the council gave up Eric and promised silver.
This is still Ripon's silver. The year Eadred burned Wilfrid's church we gave up Eric and promised to pay for the wrong. Kings forget oaths. They do not forget a sum.
Every hearth pays, and a hull that has lain here a week is a hearth. I did not make the rule. Fifty pennies is a townsman's share.
The first chest must go down to the king's men on the Humber, and the archbishop's own boat leaks. A hull that carried it would be written down differently.
There is a watch at the bend below the Foss mouth: two men and a boat. They sleep sometimes. I am only telling you where the bend is.
Pay a townsman's share, fifty pennies, though you are no townsman
Drop down the Ouse on the night ebb before he comes back
Offer your hull instead: carry the clerk and the first chest down to the king's men on the Humber
The clerk cuts your notch among the townsmen's, not the strangers'. Ulfketil says nothing about it and pays for the ale.
The ebb takes you past the bend without a sound. In the morning there is a notch against your name on the tally and no silver beside it.
The watch at the bend is awake. You are brought back up on the flood and pay the share, and a fine on top, with the whole landing looking on.
Three days down the Ouse and back, with a clerk who is sick over the side and a chest nobody may sit on. The king's man at the Humber writes down the hull that brought it.
The king with the sandal
Olaf of Dublin sits in the hall again and the Dublin ships lie three deep at the landing. Their shipmaster has more lading than hulls.
Olaf is back. They call him Cuaran, the sandal. Do not ask me why: I have heard four reasons. He was baptised in the south once, and some of it stayed on him.
I have combs and jet for Dublin and no hull to put them in. Carry them round. My partner pays on the plank path, in silver by weight.
And that is Rhine wine under your cover. The hall has drunk nothing but ale since Easter. Name three casks and I will name a price.
Carry for the Dublin men if you like. But this is the second time Olaf has sat in that hall, and I saw how he left it the first time. Quickly.
Take his lading on trust for Dublin: six bundles of combs and two of jet
Sell him three casks of Rhine wine for the hall, at the hall's price
Carry nothing of his, and ask what Dublin buys
Six bundles of antler combs and two of cut jet go under your cover on Gilli's word alone. He tells you the marks for the Liffey mouth, twice over.
Three casks go up to the hall on a sledge. Gilli pays in new pennies with the banner on them, and more of them than the market would have.
Wine, he says, and jet, and salt; and what comes back is hides, cloaks and people. He says the last word the way another man says herring.
The other end of the road
Dublin: wattle houses in fenced plots, a new bank of earth, and pens by the water. A man on the plank path knows whose hull you are before you have made fast.
You see the new bank. The Irish burned us out, not ten winters ago. We learned to dig.
Gilli's bundles? Then you are the round hull from York. Land them on the planks and I will fetch the scales.
It is hides and cloaks this year, and whatever the ships bring back. Come again after a good summer if you want to see the pens full.
The pens are full. Three thousand head came down from Kells, and their cattle with them. I have never seen people so cheap. It will not last: they die, or they are ransomed.
I kept the guest-house at Kells. I can bake, brew and say the psalms. Tell that to whoever buys, so that it is not the quern.
Land Gilli's combs and jet, every bundle
Buy two of the Kells people at the pens, cheap
Buy two and put them ashore at the church up the river
Walk the bank, count the hulls, and eat at his hearth
Every bundle is counted onto the planks. He weighs out silver in cut rings and throws in four hides, because a carrier who arrives is rarer than one who sets out.
Two of the Kells people are led aboard, a man and a boy. They do not look at you. The partner calls it a good price, and it is.
You pay the pen's price and row the two of them up to the church by the ford. The priest writes your name in a book and asks nothing about your friends.
Fenced plots along one street, a hundred hearths, and more hulls on the strand than you count at York. You eat at his fire, and after that the plot knows your face.
Eric, Harald's son
The pennies have a sword on them now. Olaf has gone back over the hills, Eric sits in the hall, and the archbishop has been taken south to the English king's prison.
Count it with me. Olaf out. Eric in. And the archbishop, who had a hand in making both, in the English king's prison. Only the moneyer is where he was.
Your Dublin friend went over the hills with Olaf. He left word that the plot on the Liffey is where it was.
I am Thorgils. I keep the king's ships, and I am taking the names of the hulls on this river. I do not write them. I remember them.
The king's peace costs forty pennies and a handshake. Without it you are a hull I have not met. I meet a great many of those at sea.
They took the archbishop south in fetters. We have a letter for him and no road. A merchant's hull goes where a priest's feet may not.
Give Eric's shipmaster your hand and forty pennies for the king's peace on the river
Take the minster's letter south, for whoever can reach the archbishop
Trade through your host and be nobody's man
Thorgils takes your hand and the silver in the same grip. The toll man is told. So is everyone else: by evening the landing knows whose peace you bought.
The letter is small, sealed twice, and sewn into a strip of calfskin. The priest gives fifteen pennies for the road and does not say who else knows of it.
You sell through Ulfketil and berth below the bridge with the fish boats. Nobody at the hall learns your name. That was the purpose.
What did you see
At London a quiet man in a good cloak has asked the port-reeve which hulls come from the Humber. He sits down on your cargo without being asked.
You come from the Humber. I do not ask what you sold. How many ships lie below the bridge at York, and whose? Who strikes the penny?
The king cannot keep meat down. He sucks the juice and leaves the rest, and still rides. A man like that does not wait long for anything.
You carry something from Saint Peter's. I can see it in how you sit. The archbishop is alive and is fed. More than that I may not say.
They tell me you gave Eric's man your hand. Hands are given. I would sooner know what the other hand is doing.
Give him the minster's letter, sealed, and ask that it reach the archbishop
Tell him what you saw: the hulls, the hall, the mint
Tell him the price of wine at York, and nothing a child could not see
He breaks neither seal and pays forty pennies for the road. His clerk shows you, on the outside, the three Latin words that say whose it is, and how to read them.
You tell him: so many hulls, so many of them long, the sword on the penny, the moneyer's name. He pays in old southern pennies, heavy ones, and forgets to thank you.
You talk of wine until he stands up. At the gangplank he says the north is dry of it this year, as if he owed you something for your time.
The rock
Below the rock of Bamburgh the high-reeve himself comes down to the beach to look at a York hull. He asks about the wine first, and then about the king.
My fathers held this rock before there were kings at York of any tongue. We will hold it after. What is in the casks?
A king who leaves York for the western sea rides by Stainmore. There is no other road for horses. Olaf's people have used it like a street.
I pay for one thing: the week the hall empties, and whether he rides or sails. A hundred pennies now. More after, from a grateful man.
You have Eric's peace on your hull. Good. Then nobody at York will wonder why you sit so near his hall.
Take his silver and agree to send word when the hall empties
Sell him what you carry and promise nothing
Hear him out, refuse the silver, and remember every word
A hundred pennies, counted by his own steward. He names a fisherman at the Tees mouth who will carry three words north faster than a horse.
He buys at a good price and does not raise the other matter again. He does not need to. You know now what is wanted, and by whom.
You push the purse back across the cask head. He looks at you a while, and then at your hull, as a man looks at a field he may buy later.
Whose men are we
Evening on the Ouse. The men have counted three kinds of penny in their pay, and the steersman has been sent aft to ask what it means.
Raven, banner, sword, and two with the English king's name. That was one week's pay. The men ask which of them will buy bread next year.
I am not asking for them. I am asking for me. When the shouting starts on this river, which bank do we row for?
They saw you give the Norwegian your hand. Half of them think that makes us safe. The other half can count kings.
And there was the purse at Bamburgh. I did not see it. I heard it when we pushed off, and so did the lookout.
Tell them all of it: whose silver you took and whose you did not
Count out twenty pennies of good weight and say the rest is your worry
Say a merchant has no king, and send him forward
You tell it in order and leave nothing out. Nobody speaks. Then the oldest hand laughs, and the steersman says the worst is known now and can be steered round.
Twenty pennies, all English, all heavy. The men bite them from habit. The question is not asked again that month.
He goes forward. The talk under the awning stops when you pass, and starts again behind you.
The hall empties
The lawmen have met without the king. By evening everyone on the landing knows it: Eric is to go, and he means to ride west over the moor with his son and his brother.
The lawmen sat this morning, the four of them, and nobody sent to the hall. That is how a king hears it here: by not being asked.
The king rides west by the moor with his son and his brother, and takes Dublin's road in spite of Dublin. The ships go round to meet him.
I need the river clear for three nights, and every round hull out of my way. Yours I would sooner have beside me than behind me.
You know something Thorgils does not: at Bamburgh a man has paid to learn the day and the road.
Keep your boat on her ropes. They will count heads this week. Be one of the heads, not one of the hulls.
Tell Thorgils the moor road is sold, and offer your hull down the Ouse by night
Send Oswulf his word: by the moor, with few men
Send to the Dublin men over the hills: the hall is empty, come before the English king's reeves
Keep the boat moored and stand with your host when the lawmen count heads

No sail, the oars wrapped, the ebb under you. A big man sits on your cargo with a boy beside him and says nothing from the bridge to the Humber. His ships are waiting at the river mouth. On Stainmore, men wait for nobody.

The townsmen have boats chained across the bend. You are turned back and fined on the landing, and the steersman has a cut scalp for his trouble. In the morning the hall is empty: he has taken the moor road.
Three words go to the fisherman at the Tees mouth. You sell that week as in any other, and you do not go near the western gate.
A rider goes over the hills with Gilli's token and a tally of what you have seen: the hall empty, the English reeves not yet come. Whatever comes of it, the English king will hear who sent.
You stand in Ulfketil's yard among his neighbours when the lawmen's man comes round, and you are counted with them. The boat does not move for a week.
No more kings
Eric is dead on Stainmore with his son and his brother. An English reeve sits in the hall, an earl from Bamburgh is over the land, and the moneyer is cutting a new die.
This year the Northumbrians expelled Eric; and King Edred took to the government of the Northumbrians.
entries.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 954, tr. J. Ingram 1823

entries.text: On Stainmore, in the empty part. A man called Maccus, Olaf's son, did the killing. The earl at Bamburgh did the knowing. The son and the brother lie with him.
Thorgils was not on the moor. He was at the Humber with the ships, cursing a chain of boats. He asked for you before he sailed, and not in anger.
The archbishop is out of prison and has a bishop's seat again: at Dorchester, far to the south. They freed the man and kept the archbishop.
There are no kings here now. There is the king. His peace is given by hand, and whoever breaks it pays more than you will see in your life.
Earl Oswulf sends a purse and his seal for a hull he names. He says you will know what for. I have not asked.
Take what the earl sends for the word you sent: silver, and his seal on the river toll
Ask the reeve for the king's peace, given by hand, on your hull and your sales
Ask nobody for anything: buy what a fallen hall sells cheap, and keep what the river has taught you

Sixteen hundred pennies, and the earl's seal on your freedom from the river toll. Ulfketil pays what he owes you that week, in full, and does not ask you in. In the Norse harbours it will be known who sold the moor road.

The reeve takes your hand before witnesses. Your hull and your sales are in the king's peace at York, free of his toll. Eight hundred pennies of old debts are paid you by men who were waiting to see who won.

The hall's goods go cheap on the landing: silk, swords, a king's bedding. You buy and sell before the price finds its feet. After these years you know every bank and shoal between the bridge and the sea.
The town keeps its own
Eric is dead on the moor and an English reeve sits in the hall. In your host's yard the men who counted heads that week are counting something else, and they have kept a place for you.
This year also Archbishop Wulfstan received a bishopric again at Dorchester.
entries.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 954, tr. J. Ingram 1823

entries.text: We counted every man who stood in this yard that week and moved no hull for any king. It was not many. It was enough to be asked what the town wants.
I have cut dies for Olaf, for Eric and for Eadred, some of them twice. This one I may be let finish. A town with one penny can sell to anybody.
The plot beside mine has no heir: its man rode west with Eric. The fence line is older than my father, and the neighbours would sooner have you than a reeve's cousin.
The minster knows who carried its letter when nobody else would. The archbishop is at Dorchester now, but his clerks are here, and clerks write things down.
Take the long plot beside his, and a seat among the men who witness sales
Take your share in silver, the seat, and his son to keep your goods here while you sail
Take the plot, and ask that the minster name you as the man who carried its letter

The fence is walked and the bounds are said aloud. Fifteen hundred pennies come to you as your share of what the yard sold while others ran. You have ground at York, a seat at the bench, and an order for ten casks.

Ulfketil's son can count, keeps his mouth shut, and is tired of his father's yard. Your goods lie under his key from now on. Eighteen hundred pennies, and a seat at the bench whenever you are in the town.
The plot is yours, and in the minster's book you are named as its man on the river. A clerk reads you the entry and makes you read it back until you can. Twelve hundred pennies besides.
A king without a town
A warship with a striped sail lies off the landing, and the man who steps ashore is one you last saw in the dark on the Ouse. He has been asking for your hull in every harbour.
Round hull. I have asked for you in six harbours. The king says a debt left unpaid goes bad like fish.
He is in the islands north of the Scots, with forty ships and no town. He says it suits him better. Towns have lawmen.
York took the English king the week we left. There is an earl now, and a penny with no sword on it.
The man at Bamburgh had riders on the moor for nine days, waiting for us. He knows whose hull we went down the river in. Stay off his beach.
Take the king's gift: a sea-going trader from his fleet, and silver to fit her
Take the arm-ring off his own arm, and the rest by weight
Ask for less silver and one thing more: that his ships let your hulls pass, and your heirs'
She lies astern of the warship: deep, broad, built to cross open sea. Taken or bought, he does not say. Nine hundred pennies to fit her out. Thorgils puts the steering oar in your hand himself.

The ring is twisted gold, as thick as a thumb, still warm from another man's arm. The rest is cut silver weighed on your own scales: eighteen hundred pennies' worth. Your grandchildren will be told where it came from.

Thorgils cuts a mark in your stem-post with his knife. Any ship of Eric's, or of his sons', that sees it will let you pass. Seven hundred pennies besides: he says the king thought you would ask for more.
One kindred, two towns
The Dublin ships came up the Humber nine days before the English king's reeves. Olaf sits in the hall at York a third time, and Gilli has been looking for you with a tally in his belt.
Nine days. We were up the Humber nine days before the English reeves, because a rider came over the hills with my token. Lawmen like a king who is there.
Eric? Dead on Stainmore. He met a son of Olaf on our road. I was not there and neither was the king, and that is what we both say.
A third time, the same Olaf. The moneyer did not even cut a new die. I do not say it will last. I say the hides are coming over the hills again.
The English king knows your hull now. He is sick and he has a long memory. Do your trading in the south under another man's name.
Swear fellowship with Gilli: one purse, his boat on the western sea and yours on the eastern
Ask the king for ground at York and freedom from his toll there
Take your share by weight, and a man on the plot at Dublin to keep your goods
You swear it on his ring and your scales: one purse, the losses halved, his boat west of the hills and yours east. Nine hundred pennies are your share of this year already.
Olaf gives ground at York the way he took the town: quickly. A plot by the river, and his word to the toll man. Seven hundred pennies besides. The word lasts as long as he does.
Thirteen hundred pennies' weight in cut silver, and from now on the man on the plank path keeps a locked chest for you by the Liffey.

The river landing at York below a timber bridge, grey morning: a moneyer in a leather apron turns silver pennies on a board; the merchant stands by his round-hulled boat; a townsman in a Danish cloak leans on a post, watching.
A York street of wattle houses at first light, the host pointing three ways: a long timber hall with carved door-posts, the stone minster behind old Roman wall, and lean Dublin ships at the landing.
The landing under a low autumn sky, a smear of smoke far to the north-west: a tonsured clerk with a tally stick and an iron-bound chest stands at the merchant's gangplank; townsmen queue with purses.

Dublin ships three deep at the York landing on a bright windy day, a banner with a three-cornered knot over the hall behind; a lean shipmaster with red-brown hair counts bundles of antler combs on the planks.

Dublin from the strand, a wet evening: fenced plots of low wattle houses, a raw earthen bank, a plank path; in front a wattle pen with people sitting in it, a woman looking straight out; ships drawn up on the mud.

The York landing in hard noon light: a broad Norwegian in a mail shirt, hands empty, looks along the row of moored hulls; behind him a longship with shields on the rail; a priest waits in a doorway with a small sewn packet.

A quay inside London's old Roman river wall, evening: a quiet man in a fine dark cloak with a silver pin sits on a wine cask in the merchant's boat; the merchant stands; a reeve looks away on the quay.

The beach under the rock of Bamburgh, the timber hall and palisade high above, cold clear morning: a tall lord in a red cloak with a gold-hilted sword looks into the beached boat; a steward holds a purse.

The boat moored on the Ouse at dusk, the awning half rigged, York's roofs and hall dark behind: the steersman stands aft with an open hand full of mixed pennies; the crew watch from forward, faces in shadow.

The king's hall at York in a summer dusk, doors open and nobody at them, saddled horses in the yard; on the landing in front, the Norwegian shipmaster and the host stand either side of the merchant, one pointing down river, one at the mooring ropes.

A bare moor road under heavy cloud with a stone cross stump and riderless horses, seen as if remembered; in front, at York, a moneyer cuts a new die at his bench while an English reeve holds out his open hand.

A long fenced plot at York running down to the river, late summer sun: townsmen walk its bounds with hazel rods, the host and the moneyer in front, the merchant between them; an empty hall roof beyond the fences.

A northern harbour in clear cold light: a warship with a red-and-white striped sail lies off; on the landing the Norwegian shipmaster holds out a twisted gold arm-ring; behind him a deep broad trading ship rides at a rope.

Lean ships crowding the Ouse below York bridge at sunrise, the knot banner over the hall again; on the landing the Dublin shipmaster grips the merchant's forearm over a pair of scales; pack-horses with hides come in at the western gate.
